title: Case study: search autocomplete
objective: Suggest searches as someone types: keep each trie node's top results ready, so a suggestion is a short walk and one read, never a search of everything below.

sources.title: Sedgewick and Wayne, Algorithms, 4th ed.: section 5.2, Tries

simplifies: A generic design, not any one search engine's. Real autocomplete also corrects typos, personalises, and filters offensive suggestions. Keeping 2 per node is to keep the trace small; real systems keep more. Counts here are tiny and illustrative.

critique.prompt: A proposal: on every keystroke, run a database query that finds every past search starting with what's typed, sorted by count; also, every search updates the counts in that same table straight away, inside the search request.

risks.text: Scanning and sorting every matching search on every keystroke is far too slow
risks.why: Precompute: keep each prefix's top results in a trie node, so a suggestion is a walk and one read.

risks.text: Updating counts inside every search request puts constant writes on the table suggestions read from
risks.why: Collect searches and rebuild the top lists in batches; suggestions can be a little behind.

risks.text: Only the top few suggestions are shown
risks.why: Nobody reads 500 suggestions; a short list is the feature.

risks.text: The browser remembers suggestions for prefixes it already asked about
risks.why: That saves repeated requests as people type and delete.

critique.hint: Count the requests: one per keystroke, from everyone typing at once.

first.prompt: Typing in the search box feels slow, and the database is at 100% CPU. Which fix comes first?

options.text: Precompute each prefix's top results, so a keystroke reads one short list
options.explanation: Right. Keystrokes far outnumber searches, so make the read cheap.
It reduces writes, but every keystroke would still scan and sort.
Sorting everything to show fewer is still sorting everything.

critique.explain: Make the frequent thing cheap: keystrokes vastly outnumber completed searches, so precompute what they read. Then move count updates off the request path into batches.

quiz.prompt: What does keeping the top results in every trie node cost?

options.text: Each new search updates a short list at every letter of its word, and every node stores a list
options.explanation: Right. Writes and memory pay so that reads are a walk plus one lookup.
Every added search touches one list per letter.
They're exact for the counts the lists were built from.

quiz.prompt: Why rebuild suggestion counts in batches instead of on every search?

options.text: Popular prefixes like a single letter would be rewritten by nearly every search; batching trades a little freshness for far fewer writes
options.explanation: Right. A suggestion a few minutes behind is usually fine.
They can; the issue is how often.

options.text: Batches make the counts more accurate
